e-9564.knowledge_point: Expressing Flux as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem in Flux Form
e-9564.problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,0), (-1,-3), (1,-3),$ and $(1,0),$  traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$\mathbf{F}(x,y) = (7x^2y^6 +x^3)\, \mathbf{i} + (- 2xy^7+4x^2y) \, \mathbf{j}$
through $C$ as a repeated integral.
e-9564.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\oint\limits_C P \,\mathrm{d}y - Q \, \mathrm{d}x = \iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \right) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/02964b07e45daba2d560fa16d34bcc92ddb8d0e0e83f644f8284dbe9d4b4557b.png)

We have that $P(x,y) =  7x^2y^6 +x^3$ and $Q(x,y) =- 2xy^7+4x^2y.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=14x{y}^{6}+3{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-14x{y}^{6}+4{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D = \{(x,y) :  -1\leq x\leq 1, \, -3\leq y \leq 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(14x{y}^{6}+3{x}^{2})+(-14x{y}^{6}+4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-3}^{0}7{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

e-9565.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle \sin(\pi y) - x , \: \cos(\pi x) + 2xy \right\rangle
$$

through the boundary of the square with vertices $(0,-1), (2,-1), (2,1),$ and $(0,1).$
e-9565.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\oint\limits_C P \,\mathrm{d}y - Q \, \mathrm{d}x = \iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \right) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/2f3374de4a29c62587a79f6286dfe788e64c37e09e9d9b83b3a67b4dac10dc21.png)

We have that $P(x,y) = \sin(\pi y) - x$ and $Q(x,y) = \cos(\pi x) + 2xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D = \left\{(x,y) :  0 \leq x \leq 2, \, -1 \leq y \leq 1 \right\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2x-1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{2}-x)\,{|}_{0}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}({2}^{2}-2)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}2\,dy \\  & =2y\,{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2(1)-2(-1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

e-9563.knowledge_point: Calculating Flux Across Other Type I and Type II Regions
e-9563.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle -3xy^2 , \: y+\cos x \right\rangle
$$

through the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0), (2,2),$ and $(-2,2).$
e-9563.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $\mathbf F = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s = \iint\limits_D \textrm{div}\,\mathbf F\,\textrm{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
\oint\limits_C P \,\mathrm{d}y - Q \, \mathrm{d}x = \iint\limits_D \left( \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y} \right) \,\textrm{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/aa822f0b9259d6d9eb5c6f439588e70d4b9bee16b2b868fae36c7cbac72d3c3f.png)

We have that $P(x,y) = -3xy^2$ and $Q(x,y) = y+\cos x .$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D = \left\{(x,y) :  -y \leq x \leq y, \, 0 \leq y \leq 2 \right\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-3{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-y}^{y}(-3{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-3{y}^{2}+1)[x]_{-y}^{y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-3{y}^{2}+1)(y-(-y))\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-3{y}^{2}+1)\cdot 2y\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(-6{y}^{3}+2y)\,dy \\  & =[-6\cdot \frac{{y}^{4}}{4}+2\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =[-\frac{3{y}^{4}}{2}+{y}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =(-24+4)-0 \\  & =-20.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the rectangle C with vertices (−1,0),(2,0),(2,2), and (−1,2), traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=x2yi+5xyj through C as a repeated integral.

a
∫02∫−12x(2y+5)dydx
b
∫−12∫02(x2−5y)dydx
c
∫−12∫02(x2+5y)dydx
d
∫02∫−12x(2y−5)dydx
e
∫−12∫02x(2y+5)dydx
Submit

decision.explanation: Green's theorem in flux form uses the divergence: ∂(x²y)/∂x + ∂(5xy)/∂y = 2xy + 5x = x(2y+5). The rectangle has −1 ≤ x ≤ 2 and 0 ≤ y ≤ 2, so option e gives the required repeated integral.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,0),(2,0),(2,2),$ and $(-1,2),$ traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$F(x,y)={x}^{2}y\,i+5xy\,j$
through $C$ as a repeated integral.
after.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/265d27ad87a7f114bd2a32a5f48cbfedb13192abf48f9b759c4ed635e71ff144.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=5xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =5x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy+5x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x(2y+5)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Consider the rectangle C with vertices (−1,0),(2,0),(2,2), and (−1,2), traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=x2yi+5xyj through C as a repeated integral.

a
∫02∫−12x(2y+5)dydx
b
∫−12∫02(x2−5y)dydx
c
∫−12∫02(x2+5y)dydx
d
∫02∫−12x(2y−5)dydx
e
∫−12∫02x(2y+5)dydx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let C be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let D be the region bounded by C. If F=Pi+Qj, and P and Q have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing D, then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

∮CF⋅nds=∬DdivFdA,

which is equivalent to ∮CPdy−Qdx=∬D(∂P∂x+∂Q∂y)dA.

The region D and the curve C for this case are shown below.

We have that P(x,y)=x2y and Q(x,y)=5xy. So,

∂P∂x=2xy,∂Q∂y=5x.

We can express the region D as a type I region as follows:

D={(x,y):−1≤x≤2,0≤y≤2}

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

∮CPdy−Qdx=∬D(∂P∂x+∂Q∂y)dA=∬D(2xy+5x)dA=∫−12∫02x(2y+5)dydx.

content.knowledge_point: Expressing Flux as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem in Flux Form
content.problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,0),(2,0),(2,2),$ and $(-1,2),$ traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$F(x,y)={x}^{2}y\,i+5xy\,j$
through $C$ as a repeated integral.
content.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/265d27ad87a7f114bd2a32a5f48cbfedb13192abf48f9b759c4ed635e71ff144.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=5xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =5x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy+5x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}x(2y+5)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
According to the flux form of Green's theorem, the flux of the vector field 
$F(x,y)=⟨y+2{x}^{2}y,\,{x}^{2}-x{y}^{2}⟩$
across the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(0,0),(2,0),(2,1),$ and  $(0,1)$ can be represented as

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, $n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C,$ and $D$ is the region bounded by $C.$ Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
after.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/98d7da0c7cd1e1f1006c1db74ae1a1e1f198d9066df6585745ee36548f0b8d96.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y+2{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the flux form of Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4xy+(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=2xy.$

content.knowledge_point: Expressing Flux as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem in Flux Form
content.problem:
According to the flux form of Green's theorem, the flux of the vector field 
$F(x,y)=⟨y+2{x}^{2}y,\,{x}^{2}-x{y}^{2}⟩$
across the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(0,0),(2,0),(2,1),$ and  $(0,1)$ can be represented as

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, $n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C,$ and $D$ is the region bounded by $C.$ Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
content.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/98d7da0c7cd1e1f1006c1db74ae1a1e1f198d9066df6585745ee36548f0b8d96.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y+2{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}-x{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the flux form of Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4xy+(-2xy))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=2xy.$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,0),(1,0),(1,2),$ and $(-1,2),$ traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$F(x,y)=3x{y}^{3}\,i+6x{y}^{4}\,j$
through $C$ as a repeated integral.
after.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/fa98f3db31860a463d0a551d5297895e61a6c041d852c04de04c44a194510961.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=3x{y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=6x{y}^{4}.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{y}^{3},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =24x{y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{y}^{3}+24x{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}3{y}^{3}(1+8x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3

Consider the rectangle C with vertices (−1,0),(1,0),(1,2), and (−1,2), traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=3xy3i+6xy4j through C as a repeated integral.

b
∫−11∫023y3(1+8x)dydx
c

d

e

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let C be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let D be the region bounded by C. If F=Pi+Qj, and P and Q have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing D, then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

∮CF⋅nds=∬DdivFdA,

which is equivalent to ∮CPdy−Qdx=∬D(∂P∂x+∂Q∂y)dA.

The region D and the curve C for this case are shown below.

We have that P(x,y)=3xy3 and Q(x,y)=6xy4. So,

∂P∂x=3y3,∂Q∂y=24xy3.

We can express the region D as a type I region as follows:

D={(x,y):−1≤x≤1,0≤y≤2}

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

∮CPdy−Qdx=∬D(∂P∂x+∂Q∂y)dA=∬D(3y3+24xy3)dA=∫−11∫023y3(1+8x)dydx.

content.knowledge_point: Expressing Flux as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem in Flux Form
content.problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,0),(1,0),(1,2),$ and $(-1,2),$ traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$F(x,y)=3x{y}^{3}\,i+6x{y}^{4}\,j$
through $C$ as a repeated integral.
content.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/fa98f3db31860a463d0a551d5297895e61a6c041d852c04de04c44a194510961.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=3x{y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=6x{y}^{4}.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{y}^{3},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =24x{y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{y}^{3}+24x{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}3{y}^{3}(1+8x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the rectangle C with vertices (0,0),(3,0),(3,2), and (0,2), traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=x2y2i+12xyj through C as a repeated integral.

a
∫03∫02(2x2+y)dydx
b
∫03∫022x(y2+6)dydx
c
∫02∫032y2(x+6)dydx
d
∫02∫03(2y2+6)dydx
e
∫02∫03(x2+12y)dydx
Submit

decision.explanation: Green's theorem in flux form uses the divergence, ∂(x²y²)/∂x + ∂(12xy)/∂y = 2xy² + 12x = 2x(y²+6). The rectangle has 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 and 0 ≤ y ≤ 2, giving option b.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(0,0),(3,0),(3,2),$ and $(0,2),$  traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$F(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,i+12xy\,j$
through $C$ as a repeated integral.
after.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/23066b23aebf332921c22a0439a414ade8dffd2a270641d186da0ed0e9488821.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=12xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =12x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le 2}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x{y}^{2}+12x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}2x({y}^{2}+6)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Consider the rectangle C with vertices (0,0),(3,0),(3,2), and (0,2), traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=x2y2i+12xyj through C as a repeated integral.

a
∫03∫02(2x2+y)dydx
b
∫03∫022x(y2+6)dydx
c
∫02∫032y2(x+6)dydx
d
∫02∫03(2y2+6)dydx
e
∫02∫03(x2+12y)dydx
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let C be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let D be the region bounded by C. If F=Pi+Qj, and P and Q have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing D, then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

∮CF⋅nds=∬DdivFdA,

which is equivalent to ∮CPdy−Qdx=∬D(∂P∂x+∂Q∂y)dA.

The region D and the curve C for this case are shown below.

We have that P(x,y)=x2y2 and Q(x,y)=12xy. So,

∂P∂x=2xy2,∂Q∂y=12x.

We can express the region D as a type I region as follows:

D={(x,y):0≤x≤3,0≤y≤2}

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

∮CPdy−Qdx=∬D(∂P∂x+∂Q∂y)dA=∬D(2xy2+12x)dA=∫03∫022x(y2+6)dydx.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms divergence 2xy²+12x=2x(y²+6), integrated over 0≤x≤3 and 0≤y≤2. Thus option b is correct; the incorrect feedback refers to the deliberately submitted option d.

content.knowledge_point: Expressing Flux as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem in Flux Form
content.problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(0,0),(3,0),(3,2),$ and $(0,2),$  traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$F(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}\,i+12xy\,j$
through $C$ as a repeated integral.
content.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/23066b23aebf332921c22a0439a414ade8dffd2a270641d186da0ed0e9488821.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=12xy.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =12x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le 2}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x{y}^{2}+12x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}2x({y}^{2}+6)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Consider the rectangle C with vertices (−3,−1),(−1,−1),(−1,1), and (−3,1), traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=(yx2+y3x)i+(−y2x+y4)j through C as a repeated integral.

a
∫−1−1∫−31(5x3+y)dydx
b
∫−3−1∫−11y3(2xy+y)dydx
c
∫−3−1∫−115y3dydx
d
∫−3−1∫−115y3(x−5)dydx
e
∫−1−1∫−315x3dydx
Submit

decision.explanation: The divergence is (2xy+y³)+(−2xy+4y³)=5y³. The rectangle is −3≤x≤−1, −1≤y≤1, so option c directly gives Green's theorem in flux form.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-3,-1),(-1,-1),(-1,1),$ and $(-3,1),$ traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$F(x,y)=(y{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}x)\,i+(-{y}^{2}x+{y}^{4})\,j$
through $C$ as a repeated integral.
after.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/5497f23e51d1e745fef1cf39d6c1a8ada22b25e8c9c7b87f5d5338e85a941739.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}x$ and $Q(x,y)=-{y}^{2}x+{y}^{4}.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2yx+{y}^{3},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2yx+4{y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-3\le x\le -1,\,-1\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2yx+{y}^{3})+(-2yx+4{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{-1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}5{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Consider the rectangle C with vertices (−3,−1),(−1,−1),(−1,1), and (−3,1), traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=(yx2+y3x)i+(−y2x+y4)j through C as a repeated integral.

a
∫−1−1∫−31(5x3+y)dydx
b
∫−3−1∫−11y3(2xy+y)dydx
c
∫−3−1∫−115y3dydx
d
∫−3−1∫−115y3(x−5)dydx
e
∫−1−1∫−315x3dydx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let C be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let D be the region bounded by C. If F=Pi+Qj, and P and Q have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing D, then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

∮CF⋅nds=∬DdivFdA,

which is equivalent to ∮CPdy−Qdx=∬D(∂P∂x+∂Q∂y)dA.

The region D and the curve C for this case are shown below.

We have that P(x,y)=yx2+y3x and Q(x,y)=−y2x+y4. So,

∂P∂x=2yx+y3,∂Q∂y=−2yx+4y3.

We can express the region D as a type I region as follows:

D={(x,y):−3≤x≤−1,−1≤y≤1}

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

∮CPdy−Qdx=∬D(∂P∂x+∂Q∂y)dA=∬D(2yx+y3)+(−2yx+4y3)dA=∫−3−1∫−115y3dydx.

content.knowledge_point: Expressing Flux as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem in Flux Form
content.problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-3,-1),(-1,-1),(-1,1),$ and $(-3,1),$ traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$F(x,y)=(y{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}x)\,i+(-{y}^{2}x+{y}^{4})\,j$
through $C$ as a repeated integral.
content.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/5497f23e51d1e745fef1cf39d6c1a8ada22b25e8c9c7b87f5d5338e85a941739.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}x$ and $Q(x,y)=-{y}^{2}x+{y}^{4}.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2yx+{y}^{3},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2yx+4{y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-3\le x\le -1,\,-1\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2yx+{y}^{3})+(-2yx+4{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{-1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}5{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=⟨ey+2x2y,ex+2xy2⟩ through the boundary of the rectangle with vertices (−1,0),(2,0),(2,1), and (−1,1).

a
8
b
4
c
10
d
2
e
6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let C be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let D be the region bounded by C. If F=Pi+Qj, and P and Q have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing D, then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

∮CF⋅nds=∬DdivFdA,

which is equivalent to ∮CPdy−Qdx=∬D(∂P∂x+∂Q∂y)dA.

The region D and the curve C for this case are shown below.

We have that P(x,y)=ey+2x2y and Q(x,y)=ex+2xy2. So,

∂P∂x=4xy,∂Q∂y=4xy.

We can express the rectangular region D as follows:

D={(x,y):−1≤x≤2,0≤y≤1}

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx=∬D(∂P∂x+∂Q∂y)dA=∬D(4xy+4xy)dA=∫01∫−128xydxdy=∫014x2y|−12dy=∫01(4(2)2y−4(−1)2y)dy=∫01(16y−4y)dy=∫0112ydy=6y2|01=6.

content.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{y}+2{x}^{2}y,\,{e}^{x}+2x{y}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the rectangle with vertices $(-1,0),(2,0),(2,1),$ and $(-1,1).$
content.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/f6437eddec7d44a10c7fb2b3461a09844ca06e5131b69503f51432eb87fedd31.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{y}+2{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{x}+2x{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4xy+4xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{2}8xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{x}^{2}y\,{|}_{-1}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4(2)^{2}y-4(-1)^{2}y)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(16y-4y)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}12y\,dy \\  & =6{y}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨6{x}^{2}+2y,\,-10y-\operatorname{arctan}⁡x⟩
$$

through the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(2,1),$ and $(-2,1).$
after.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/3ad0a876fe801980a2c3724a639fc6c379db750635c0278a10a5094e2d64c34a.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=6{x}^{2}+2y$ and $Q(x,y)=-10y-\operatorname{arctan}⁡x.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=12x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-2y\le x\le 2y,\,0\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(12x-10)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2y}^{2y}(12x-10)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[6{x}^{2}-10x]_{-2y}^{2y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(24{y}^{2}-20y)-(24{y}^{2}+20y)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-40y)\,dy \\  & =-40{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-40(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =-20.\end{aligned}
$$

Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field F(x,y)=⟨xy−y2+1,x3+y⟩ through the boundary of the triangle with vertices (0,0),(1,2), and (−1,2).

a
2
b
143
c
−4
d
53
e
−112
Submit

decision.explanation: The divergence is y+1. The triangle has 0≤y≤2 and −y/2≤x≤y/2, so the flux is ∫₀²∫₋ᵧ/₂ᵞ/₂(y+1) dx dy = ∫₀²(y²+y) dy = 8/3+2 = 14/3.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨xy-\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1},\,{x}^{3}+y⟩
$$

through the boundary of the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(1,2),$ and $(-1,2).$
after.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/006d80a7dbe4d03b78cc5fb1a642405e3fdfdd69ec9d80014ee8e0355ad1ae73.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=xy-\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{3}+y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \frac{y}{2},\,0\le y\le 2}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-y/2}^{y/2}(y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(y+1)[x]_{-y/2}^{y/2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(y+1)[\frac{y}{2}-(-\frac{y}{2})]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}+y)\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{4}{2})-0 \\  & =\frac{14}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
D={(x,y):\sqrt{y}\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 1}

$$

EXPLANATION

Let C be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let D be the region bounded by C. If F=Pi+Qj, and P and Q have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing D, then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

∮CF⋅nds=∬DdivFdA, which is equivalent to ∮CPdy−Qdx=∬D(∂P∂x+∂Q∂y)dA.

The region D and the curve C for this case are shown below.

We have that P(x,y)=30xy and Q(x,y)=15y2−sin⁡x. Therefore,

∂P∂x=30y,∂Q∂y=30y.

We can express the region D as a type II region as follows:

D={(x,y):y≤x≤y,0≤y≤1}

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

∮CF⋅nds=∮CPdy−Qdx=∬D(∂P∂x+∂Q∂y)dA=∬D(30y+30y)dA=∫01∫−yy60ydxdy=60∫01y[x]−yydy=60∫01y(y+y)dy=60∫01(y2+y3/2)dy=60[y33+2y5/25]01=60(13+25)−0=44.

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Flux Across Other Type I and Type II Regions
content.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨30xy,\,15{y}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $x=y,$ $\,x=-\sqrt{y},$ and the line $y=1.$
content.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14062447/assets/24369439bc62cf06084a43d97dff0cee4e4089fd103511ef73d9dd5af1256ebb.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=30xy$ and $Q(x,y)=15{y}^{2}-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=30y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =30y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):\sqrt{y}\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(30y+30y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{y}}^{y}60y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =60{\int }_{0}^{1}y[x]_{-\sqrt{y}}^{y}\,dy \\  & =60{\int }_{0}^{1}y(y+\sqrt{y})\,dy \\  & =60{\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}+{y}^{3/2})\,dy \\  & =60{[\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+\frac{2{y}^{5/2}}{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =60(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{2}{5})-0 \\  & =44.\end{aligned}
$$
